title: Mismatch between Raman shear modes and ferroelectric polarization in 3R-MoS$_{2}$
authors: Johannes Schwandt-Krause, Jan-Niklas Heidkamp, Mohammed El Amine Miloudi, Swarup Deb, Elisabeth Grune, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Rico Schwartz, Oliver Kühn, Tobias Korn
abstract: Sliding ferroelectricity in parallel-stacked two-dimensional van der Waals materials enables a broad range of novel device concepts, but exploiting it requires reliable, non-destructive assignment of the underlying stacking order and polarization state. Here, we combine Kelvin-probe force microscopy (KPFM) with low-frequency Raman spectroscopy to probe the polarization domains and stacking configurations of a exfoliated trilayer 3R-MoS$_{2}$ flake on a hBN substrate. We find that ABA and BAB - both stackings with zero net polarization - are indistinguishable in KPFM, yet show drastically different low-frequency shear modes. This observation is reproduced across multiple flakes and is corroborated by low-temperature photoluminescence. Notably, the standard bond-polarizability model does not account for the difference in shear-mode activity between the ABA and BAB configurations, indicating that the interlayer Raman response of these stackings is governed by physics beyond a simple polarizability picture. Our results show that none of the here-used individual techniques alone is sufficient to assign sliding-ferroelectric stacking order and motivate a combined spectroscopic-scanning-probe approach.
summary: This work demonstrates that characterizing ferroelectric stacking order in layered $	ext{MoS}_2$ requires combining multiple advanced techniques. KPFM alone fails to distinguish between certain neutral stackings (ABA vs. BAB), but the combination of low-frequency Raman spectroscopy and PL successfully resolves these ambiguities by probing complementary structural, vibrational, and electronic properties.
main_problem: The core challenge is achieving reliable, non-destructive assignment of the stacking order and ferroelectric polarization state in sliding ferroelectric van der Waals materials like trilayer 3R-MoS2.
main_result: A combined approach using KPFM, low-frequency Raman spectroscopy, and photoluminescence is necessary because no single technique can uniquely determine the local structural or electronic configuration of the material.
method: The study combines Kelvin-probe force microscopy (KPFM) to map surface potential, low-frequency Raman spectroscopy to probe shear modes sensitive to interlayer coupling, and photoluminescence (PL) to analyze excitonic signatures.
model_or_system: The system is exfoliated trilayer 3R-MoS2 flakes on an hBN substrate. The analysis compares different stacking configurations (e.g., ABA vs. BAB), which exhibit distinct physical properties despite some being indistinguishable by electrostatic measurements alone.
key_observables: Surface potential contrast ($	ext{KPFM}$); low-frequency Raman shear mode intensities ($	ext{S}1$ and $	ext{S}2$); A-exciton spectral line shapes ($	ext{PL}$).
important_parameters: The distinction between zero net polarization stackings (ABA/BAB) versus polar ones (ABC), and the failure of simple bond-polarizability models to explain all observed Raman shifts.
main_assumptions: Individual techniques are insufficient; a complementary, multi-modal spectroscopic-scanning-probe approach is required for full characterization.
figures_summary: Figures compare KPFM maps with Raman intensity maps across different domains (I vs II) and show PL spectra taken from representative stacking regions ($	ext{ABC}$, $	ext{ABA}$, $	ext{BAB}$) to demonstrate the unique signatures of each technique.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the need for characterization, presents data showing KPFM ambiguity between certain stackings (ABA/BAB), then uses Raman spectroscopy to resolve this degeneracy by observing different shear modes. Finally, PL is used to further distinguish between these spectroscopically similar but structurally distinct domains.
why_interesting: While not directly quantum information related, the study of polarization switching and structural characterization in 2D materials touches upon emergent collective electronic states and lattice dynamics that are crucial for designing solid-state quantum devices.

figures.caption: Figure 1: (a) Optical micrograph of the 3R-MoS2/hBN flake showing the regions of differing layer number. The white bar denotes 5 µm. (b) High-frequency Raman spectra of the 2L and 3L regions, where the E2g–A1g separation (∆ω2L ≈23 cm−1, ∆ω3L ≈24 cm−1) confirms the layer assignment. The spectra are taken at representative coloured spots marked in (a). (c) Room-temperature photoluminescence spectrum deconvolved into the interlayer (IX), A-exciton (XA), and B-exciton (XB) contributions. (d-f) Spatially-resolved PL-intensity maps of the flake for the A-exciton (d), B-exciton (e) and interlayer exciton (f).

Figure 2: (a) KPFM surface-potential map of the 3L part of the MoS2 flake alongside Raman-intensity maps of the shear-modes. (b) Stokes/anti-Stokes low-frequency Raman spectra for two regions of the flake (Region I, red; Region II, blue), resolving the S1 and S2 interlayer shear modes. Inset crystal-structure schematics indicate the candidate stacking sequences and displacement associated with each region/shear mode. (c) S1 and (d) S2, showing the spatial correlation between ferroelectric domains (n1/n2 denote neutral domains, p denotes a polar domain) and shear-mode activity of different modes across the sample. The white bars denote 5 µm.

Figure 3: (a) KPFM surface-potential map and the corresponding low-frequency Raman-intensity maps of the shear modes (b) S1 and (c) S2 of a the same flake as in Fig. 1 and Fig. 2 after an annealing procedure. The white bars denote 5 µm. (d) Photoluminescence intensity map of the A exciton transition of the same area as in (b) and (c) at low temperatures (4 K). (e) Photoluminescence spectra taken at three representative positions (ABC, ABA and BAB domain, respectively) show the variation in XA lineshape and the relative weight of the higher-energy feature between domains. The color of the plots matches the inset color markings shown in (a).
